card.name: Gigue
card.era: 17th c. (imported into France from the British/Irish jig); Baroque suite movement
card.tagline: Lively Baroque suite-closing dance; the French form of the jig.
card.profile: The gigue (Italian giga) is a lively Baroque dance originating from the British/Irish jig, imported into France in the mid-17th century, where it usually appears as the final movement of the instrumental suite (Wikipedia; Britannica). It is usually in 3/8 or a compound metre (6/8, 6/4, 9/8, 12/8), often in fugal/contrapuntal texture with accents on the third beats. The French gigue was light and ornamented; the Italian giga faster and more virtuosic. The gigue was probably never a court dance but was danced by nobility on social occasions; in early French theatre, performances customarily ended with a gigue. Bach's suites and Pachelbel's 'Canon and Gigue' are well-known examples.
card.insight: This is primarily a musical form / stylized concert dance rather than a living folk dance - Britannica notes true jigs were quick and wild solo dances while gigues were danced by couples in formal ballet style (Britannica).
